column1: insight

Products: only 5 of the top-10 products by units are also in the top-10 by revenue. Popcorn Holder leads in units (~56k) but ranks 10 by revenue; Regency Cakestand 3 Tier leads revenue (~164k) but ranks 44 by units. Price per unit, not just volume, decides what drives revenue.

Time: revenue from Sep-Nov 2011 is ~3.5M, about 36% of the whole period, and Nov 2011 (1.43M) is ~2.3x the Jan-Aug monthly average (~634k). Descriptive only: with ~1 year of data we cannot call it a recurring seasonal pattern, and Dec 2011 is incomplete (ends on the 9th).

Customers: the top 20% of identifiable customers generate 74% of identified revenue, and 30.4% of customers bought only once. Revenue is concentrated, and a large share of customers never came back in the observed period.
Hours/days: revenue peaks in the hours 10:00-15:59 (top hours: 12, 10, 15, 13, 11) and no transactions are recorded on Saturday.

Countries: the UK accounts for 3,942 of the 4,362 identified customers and 84.8% of net product revenue. Outside the UK, average order value varies widely: Netherlands ~3,048 and Australia ~2,445 (9 and 9 customers) vs Germany ~453 and France ~477 (95 and 87 customers). International revenue comes from two patterns: a few large buyers vs many UK-sized buyers. Whether the large ones are wholesalers needs the basket-size analysis.

Returns: returned value is 4.6% of gross product sales and 14.8% of invoices are cancellations. Two orders (StockCodes 23166 and 23843 by customers 12346 and 16446) of ~74-81k units were cancelled 12-16 minutes after being placed; they are 51.7% of returned value. Without them returns are 2.3% of gross sales.

Returns vs price: the value return rate rises with price (1.34% in the cheapest quartile to 2.68% in the priciest, excluding the two reversals). Descriptive only: the data does not support 'pricier products are returned less'. Product type or buyer type may explain it.
Pareto: 841 of 3,905 products (21.5%) generate 80% of net revenue; the top 20% generate 78.3%. Revenue is concentrated in a minority of SKUs, with a long tail of low-contribution products.

Baskets: the top 10% of invoices (value >= ~911) generate 47.3% of revenue, with median value ~1,498 vs ~270 for the rest. This is a bulk-like signal, not proof of wholesale: 82% of these invoices are still UK.

Dead stock: 22 of 921 high-volume products (2.4%) had zero sales in the last 90 days, but they represent only 0.7% of historical revenue. The issue is small; some may be seasonal since the window and the data end on 9 Dec.

Heatmap: the single strongest slot is Thursday at 10:00 (291k, 2.9% of purchase revenue); Tuesday and Thursday together carry 42% of weekday-hour revenue. Maintenance should avoid these peaks, and ad timing can be tested around them.
RFM: Champions are 18.0% of customers but 63.2% of revenue (median 9 orders, avg recency 11 days).
RFM: At-Risk High-Value customers (319) have spent 6.7% of revenue but have been inactive for ~130 days on average: the most valuable win-back target.
RFM: Lost / Hibernating is 31.0% of customers and only 7.3% of revenue, so retention budget should not go here first.

Whales: 39 customers (0.9%) generate 27.9% of identified spend (median 46 orders, recency 4 days). They behave like trade accounts, but the data cannot confirm it. The count depends on the DBSCAN eps (31 to 61 customers, 26-32% of spend).
Concentration: Whales + Core Loyal are 18.0% of customers but 67.2% of identified spend, while Recent Light Buyers + Dormant One-Timers are 54.7% of customers and only 10.8% of spend.

Rule-based RFM puts Whales and Core Loyal together in 'Champions', but median spend differs 13x (42,056 vs 3,191). 4 whales are rule-labelled At-Risk or Lost (spend 72,776): the highest-value win-back targets.

Due-Now Regulars (1183 customers, 22.0% of spend) have median recency 56 days, about their usual gap between orders; 45% of the repeat buyers are already past their own gap. A timely reorder reminder is a hypothesis worth testing before they lapse.
Dormant One-Timers are 35.6% of customers but 6.1% of spend, inactive for a median 184 days. Heavy discounting here is hard to justify on value alone.

Whale silence in real days: 5 of 39 whales have not ordered for more than 30 days (longest: 275 days), while the median whale ordered 4 days ago. Their usual gap is only ~5 days, so a ratio to the gap would overstate the problem.
